strapline: Three term-limit petitions and a minister who will not speak for the President; Hichilema in Choma; NHIMA on gross pay; the raid video stays; and a draw in Ndola

stories.title: Three petitions and no sponsor: Mwiimbu says the government will not interfere with calls to remove term limits, and will not say whether Hichilema would sign one
stories.excerpt: Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu told a Lusaka press briefing on Friday 13 November that three petitions asking Parliament to amend Article 106(3), the two-term limit, were initiated by citizens and are not sponsored by President Hichilema, the UPND or the government, which will leave the National Assembly to handle them. Asked whether the President would back an amendment if MPs passed one, he said he could not speak for him. UPND legal chairperson Mulambo Haimbe says the party has never discussed the matter.

image.label: Article 106(3)
image.caption: The Justice Minister says three citizens' petitions on the presidential term limit are Parliament's business, not the executive's.

body: The government has put a formal position on the record in the argument over presidential term limits, and it is one of distance. Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu told journalists at a press briefing in Lusaka on Friday 13 November that three petitions have been submitted to the National Assembly seeking to amend Article 106(3) of the Constitution, the clause that limits a president to two terms, and that the executive will not interfere with how Parliament deals with them. The Times of Zambia, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer all reported the briefing.

According to the Times of Zambia, the petitions came from members of the public, political leaders and civil society organisations. Mwiimbu said the government **"respects the constitutional right of citizens to petition the National Assembly"**, the paper reported, and that the Assembly is the institution mandated to consider what they raise. The Zambian Observer reported him citing Article 88(1), which gives citizens the right to petition Parliament, and saying that Parliament is independent of the executive.

The Zambian Observer reported that Mwiimbu categorically denied that President Hakainde Hichilema or the United Party for National Development was behind the petitions, and dismissed suggestions that the President was quietly encouraging a campaign. In the Observer's account he said the petitioners had acted on their own constitutional rights, and he urged leaders to stop misleading the public and to let lawful processes run. News Diggers reported him saying that any interference by the executive would itself be unconstitutional, that the government had no role in the petitions or the proposals, and that it would not be distracted from its Grow Zambia Agenda by political speculation.

The question that the briefing did not settle was the President's own view. Asked whether Hichilema would support an amendment if Parliament approved one, Mwiimbu declined to speculate and said he could not speak for the President, the Zambian Observer reported.

body.text: The party line, and the civil society warning

body: A day earlier, News Diggers carried an interview with Mulambo Haimbe, the UPND's deputy chairperson for legal affairs, who said that **"at no point had the UPND, as a party, ever held discussions relating to the removal of presidential term limits"**. He was responding to Josiah Kalala, executive director of the Chapter One Foundation, who had said on Monday 9 November that civil society would consider legal action if there were attempts to remove the limit. Haimbe called it inappropriate to threaten litigation over a change the government had not proposed, and said citizens had a constitutional right to express views on possible amendments whether or not others agreed with them.

The petitions land in an argument that has been running for a week. On Thursday 12 November, as Zambia Monitor reported, ten of the candidates defeated by Hichilema in the election of 13 August 2026, among them Harry Kalaba, Fred M'membe and Kelvin Bwalya, issued a joint statement in Lusaka opposing any removal of the limit, declaring that **"Zambia does not belong to an individual, a political party or an administration"**. Zambia Monitor attributes the proposal they were answering to Mwato Kabaso, a nominated Member of Parliament representing the youth. The Zambian Observer reported that opposition parties and civil society organisations fear the change would weaken safeguards against prolonged presidential rule.

body.title: Who has said what
items: **Jack Mwiimbu, Justice Minister, Friday 13 November** — three petitions are before the National Assembly; the government will not interfere and is not behind them; he cannot speak for the President on whether he would back an amendment
**Mulambo Haimbe, UPND legal chairperson, Wednesday 11 November** — the party has never discussed removing term limits
**Josiah Kalala, Chapter One Foundation, Monday 9 November** — civil society would consider legal action if an attempt were made
**Ten defeated presidential candidates, Thursday 12 November** — joint statement against removing the two-term limit

body.confirmed: That three petitions seeking to amend Article 106(3) have been submitted to the National Assembly, and that the Justice Minister told a Lusaka press briefing on Friday 13 November that the government is not behind them and will not interfere, is reported by the Times of Zambia, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer. Haimbe's statement that the UPND has never discussed the matter is reported by News Diggers.
body.unverified: Who exactly signed the three petitions and what they ask for in detail has not been published by the outlets cited. President Hichilema has not stated his own position on an amendment; his minister declined to speak for him. Whether the National Assembly will table the petitions, and on what timetable, is not yet known.

stories.title: 'How can we be unpopular?': in Choma, Hichilema points to 14 by-election wins, promises a dual carriageway to the south and says FRA money will arrive within 10 to 15 days
stories.excerpt: Addressing a public engagement in Choma on Friday 13 November, President Hichilema dismissed talk on social media that the UPND is losing support, citing its sweep of all 14 seats contested in the by-elections of 5 November. He promised a dual carriageway from Lusaka into Southern Province on the Lusaka–Ndola model, said farmers owed by the Food Reserve Agency would be paid within 10 to 15 days, and warned teachers and nurses who refuse rural postings that they risk their jobs. The Times of Zambia and News Diggers reported the event.

image.label: Choma, Friday
image.caption: The President told a Choma crowd that by-election results, not TikTok, measure his party's standing.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema used a public engagement in Choma on Friday 13 November to answer the claim, which he said circulates on TikTok, that his party is losing popularity. News Diggers reported him asking how the United Party for National Development could be unpopular when it had won all 14 seats contested in the by-elections of 5 November. The Times of Zambia, which said thousands of residents and supporters attended, reported him describing those wins, spread across eight provinces, as a sign of public confidence, and thanking Zambians for renewing his mandate in the August general election.

The Times reported that he said his second term would concentrate on job creation through the Grow Zambia Agenda. News Diggers reported a specific promise for Southern Province: a dual carriageway linking it to Lusaka, built on the model of the Lusaka–Ndola dual carriageway.

On the maize farmers still waiting to be paid by the Food Reserve Agency, the Times of Zambia reported the President saying that outstanding payments would be made within 10 to 15 days and that the government had secured the money to clear every farmer owed across the country. He urged farmers not to sell all their maize and to keep some for the household. The paper also reported him announcing a programme of strategic dams across the country to provide water for people and livestock as a response to climate change, and saying Zambia would overcome the effects of the El Niño phenomenon.

The President's words, as the Times reported them, describe when farmers can expect to have been paid rather than when the first transfers go out; neither outlet reported how much is outstanding or how many farmers are still waiting.

Both outlets reported a pointed message to public servants. News Diggers said the President warned teachers and nurses who have refused to report to rural duty stations that they risk losing their jobs. The Times of Zambia reported him calling on teachers, nurses and agricultural officers to commit to their work, cautioning nurses against spending working hours on social media, and urging citizens to report officers who fail to deliver services. Neither outlet's visible text names the rural postings he had in mind or says how many workers have declined them.

News Diggers' account quotes the President beginning a sentence with the by-elections: **"On the 5th of November, there were by-elections in eight..."**, the visible text ending there. The full speech has not been published by either outlet.

stories.title: Two per cent of everything: Cabinet moves the NHIMA deduction from basic to gross pay from January 2027, as the Treasury takes on the scheme's K1.7 billion debt and dialysis bill
stories.excerpt: Health Minister Roma Chilengi said on ZNBC's main news on Thursday 12 November that Cabinet has approved calculating the 2% National Health Insurance contribution on total salary rather than basic pay, part of a rescue of a scheme he said was set up on flawed financial grounds. The government will absorb K1.7 billion NHIMA owes hospitals and suppliers, pay directly for kidney dialysis that has cost the fund about K400 million a year, and contribute for elderly people who do not pay in. The changes take effect with the 2027 budget in January.

image.label: NHIMA, recalculated
image.caption: From January the health insurance deduction will be taken from gross salary, and the State will carry the scheme's old debts.

body: Workers will see a larger National Health Insurance deduction on their payslips from January 2027. Health Minister Professor Roma Chilengi, speaking on ZNBC TV1's main news on Thursday 12 November, said Cabinet had approved a transition so that the 2% contribution to the National Health Insurance Management Authority is worked out on gross pay rather than basic pay. News Diggers and the Zambian Observer, the latter carrying a ZANIS report, covered the announcement.

The Zambian Observer quoted the minister's summary: **"Workers will now pay two percent of their total salary, not just two percent of basic pay."** Neither outlet reported any change to the employer's share.

body.text: A rescue, not just a rate change

body: Chilengi framed the move as part of a wider effort to stop NHIMA sinking under debt. News Diggers reported him saying the government had stepped in because the scheme was established on flawed financial grounds and could not meet its obligations. The Zambian Observer listed the other measures Cabinet approved: the government will take over the K1.7 billion that NHIMA owes to hospitals and health suppliers; it will begin paying contributions on behalf of elderly citizens who do not contribute; part of the Social Cash Transfer allocation will be used to buy health insurance for beneficiaries; and the State will pay directly for kidney dialysis, a service the Observer said has cost NHIMA about K400 million a year.

The measures start in January 2027, when the next national budget takes effect, the Observer reported. The same budget proposes raising VAT from 16% to 16.5%, a change the IMF's resident representative Reginald Darius told a ZIPAR panel on Thursday 12 November would raise revenue provided compliance and administration improve, News Diggers reported; the NHIMA change adds a second item to what wage earners will see change in January.

News Diggers also reported a second, separate remark from the same broadcast: Chilengi said that health workers who had been retired in the national interest could have been politically inclined during the general election of 13 August. The outlet's visible text does not say how many workers were affected or what evidence the minister cited, and the remark has not been reported in detail elsewhere.

stories.title: The raid video stays, two paragraphs go: the High Court splits the DPP's objection in the Mundubile and Zulu bail case, and a defence lawyer says three of the 18 could walk
stories.excerpt: The bench of Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga ruled on Friday 13 November that the flash disk carrying footage of the raid on Makebi Zulu's home stays on the record of the constitutional bail application by Brian Mundubile, Zulu and 16 others, while striking paragraphs 6 and 21 of their affidavit in reply and keeping 19, 20 and 22. The DPP had wanted all five paragraphs and the video out. Defence lawyer Milner Katolo told News Diggers that Bishop Trevor Mwamba and two others could be released or become State witnesses.

image.label: Five paragraphs, one disk
image.caption: The court admitted the raid footage and removed two paragraphs; whether the 18 get bail is still to be decided.

body: The ruling the Lusaka High Court promised for Friday 13 November has gone partly each way. The bench of Justices Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga admitted the flash disk containing video footage of the raid at Makebi Zulu's residence into the record of the constitutional bail application brought by Brian Mundubile, Zulu and 16 co-applicants, but struck two of the five paragraphs of their affidavit in reply that Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri SC had objected to. The Zambian Observer reported the ruling in two pieces on Friday; News Diggers carried the defence's reading of it on Saturday.

According to the Zambian Observer's account, the State had argued that the affidavit in reply introduced fresh matters it had no chance to answer, and asked the court to expunge paragraphs 6, 19, 20, 21 and 22 together with the disk. The court removed paragraph 6, finding it raised a new issue in breach of the rules on affidavits in reply, and paragraph 21, which it found went beyond the issues raised by the DPP as second respondent. Paragraphs 19 and 20 stayed because they directly answered the State's allegation that the applicants were a flight risk, and paragraph 22 stayed too. The State had separately questioned the foundation laid for the recording, the Observer reported, but the video was admitted. The ruling settles only what is on the record; it does not decide whether the 18 should be released.

body.text: What the defence takes from it

body: News Diggers reported defence lawyer Milner Katolo saying the court had rejected the DPP's application to remove the video of the raid at Zulu's house. Katolo went further, telling the outlet that Bishop Trevor Mwamba and two other accused could be released or turned into State witnesses, because the police had taken ordinary statements from them rather than warn-and-caution statements, the form used when a person is being treated as a suspect. That is the lawyer's argument, not a finding of the court, and the State has not been reported responding to it.

The 18 applicants, held at Mukobeko Maximum Security Correctional Facility, have been in custody since 14 August 2026 over alleged treason, sedition and terrorism-related offences, the Zambian Observer reported earlier in the week. They have sued Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha and the DPP, seeking unconditional release or bail on reasonable conditions and arguing that continued detention violates their constitutional rights. On Tuesday 10 November the same bench dismissed a separate State objection that had challenged their route to the court, finding no law or rule barred an aggrieved person from seeking constitutional bail this way; the DPP's objection to the video followed a day later. Mundubile stood for president in August and Zulu was his running mate; all 18 are presumed innocent, and the charges have not been tested at trial.

body.confirmed: That the bench struck paragraphs 6 and 21, kept 19, 20 and 22, and admitted the flash disk is reported by the Zambian Observer; News Diggers reports the defence's account that the video application was rejected. Both outlets state that bail itself has not been decided.
body.unverified: Katolo's claim that three of the accused could be released or become witnesses is his own assessment and has not been confirmed by the court or the State. The outlets cited do not give the date on which the bench will rule on bail, nor what the admitted footage shows beyond a raid at Zulu's home.

stories.title: The court goes to the patient: Judge Mulenga visits Jay Jay Banda at Maina Soko after a surgeon's report of a shattered shinbone, with the habeas corpus ruling still to come
stories.excerpt: After the State failed to bring former Petauke Central MP Emmanuel 'Jay Jay' Banda to court, High Court Judge Geoffrey Mulenga went to Maina Soko Military Medical Centre on Friday 13 November to see his condition for himself. Surgeon Dr Charles Mukunta's report says Banda had major surgery on 24 October to fix a severe fracture of the left shinbone near the knee with a plate and screws and must not bear weight on the leg. His mother, who brought the habeas corpus application, says she fears he will never walk again.

image.label: Maina Soko
image.caption: A High Court judge went to the military hospital to check on a detainee the State said could not be moved.

body: The habeas corpus proceedings over Emmanuel Jay Jay Banda moved from the courtroom to the hospital ward on Friday 13 November. News Diggers reported that High Court Judge Geoffrey Mulenga visited the Maina Soko Military Medical Centre in Lusaka to assess the health of the former Petauke Central Member of Parliament, after the State had failed to produce him for the hearing and his treating doctor had refused to let him be moved. The Zambian Observer reported that the Attorney General had applied for the court to move to the hospital, and that Banda's lawyer, Nkula Botha, accompanied the court.

The visit followed the medical report the judge had demanded earlier in the week. According to News Diggers, orthopaedic surgeon Dr Charles Mukunta reported that Banda remains admitted and must not put weight on his injured leg after major surgery to repair a severely fractured shinbone near the knee. The Zambian Observer gave the detail from the court documents: a Schatzker VI fracture of the left tibial plateau, with breaks to the tibia and fibula and damage to the knee joint, fixed on 24 October 2026 with a locking plate and screws. X-ray images and photographs of the surgical stitches were among the papers filed, the Observer reported.

The Zambian Observer stressed that the visit was to establish Banda's condition independently and was not a decision on the habeas corpus application itself; it said a ruling is forthcoming but gave no date, and News Diggers' visible text gives none either. Banda, 41, was apprehended in Mozambique on 14 October 2026, according to the Observer, and his mother, Grace Nampokolwe Banda, filed the application on 30 October.

In a separate piece on Saturday the Zambian Observer carried an interview that Banda's mother gave to Zambian Watch after visiting him. **"I saw him yesterday at Maina Soko Military Hospital, and I can tell you that my son will never walk again,"** she said, adding that he was in great pain and that his leg was terribly broken. She said she was relieved he was alive despite speculation on social media, and that she wished the situation that led to his detention had been handled differently. Her account of his prognosis is her own; the surgeon's report, as reported, describes post-operative recovery and a bar on bearing weight, not a permanent outcome.

The outlets cited do not describe the events behind Banda's injuries or the matters for which he is held, and no court has made findings on them. Earlier in the week the State had failed to produce him for the hearing; the judge responded by ordering the medical report that led to Friday's visit.

body.confirmed: That Judge Mulenga visited Maina Soko on Friday 13 November, that Banda had surgery on 24 October for a severe fracture of the left shinbone and may not bear weight, and that the habeas corpus application was filed by his mother on 30 October, is reported by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer.
body.unverified: The date of the ruling on the application has not been reported. The mother's statement that her son will never walk again is her own view and is not in the surgeon's report as reported. How Banda sustained the injury has not been set out by the outlets cited.

stories.title: £3 billion in and more promised: at the King's birthday reception Britain's envoy pledges investment for Grow Zambia, and the mines minister asks for help towards 3 million tonnes
stories.excerpt: British High Commissioner Rebecca Terzeon told guests at the British Residence in Lusaka that UK investment stock in Zambia exceeds £3 billion, that the UK–Zambia Green Growth Compact has drawn £1.6 billion of UK-linked investment since 2021 and that £15 million for the Zambia–Tanzania interconnector helped unlock US$300 million from the World Bank and the EU. Mines Minister Brenda Tambatamba asked for British money in mining, energy and critical minerals, saying new discoveries, not just bigger mines, are needed to hit the 2031 copper target.

image.label: The British Residence
image.caption: Britain counts its Zambian investment at more than £3 billion and says it is shifting from delivering services to sharing expertise.

body: The annual celebration of the Official Birthday of King Charles III at the British Residence in Lusaka doubled as an investment pitch from both sides. British High Commissioner Rebecca Terzeon said the United Kingdom's investment stock in Zambia now exceeds £3 billion, making it one of the country's largest investors, Zambia Monitor reported on Saturday 14 November. **"The United Kingdom remains a committed and natural partner for Zambia,"** she said, echoing a description Zambia Monitor said President Hichilema himself had used.

Terzeon set out the figures Britain wants credit for. According to Zambia Monitor, the UK–Zambia Green Growth Compact has attracted an additional £1.6 billion in UK-linked investment since 2021; a £15 million British contribution to the Zambia–Tanzania power interconnector helped unlock a further US$300 million from the World Bank and the European Union; and British International Investment has backed small and medium-sized enterprises and acted as anchor investor in Zambia's first sustainability bond. She said the UK was ready to bring investment, expertise and partnerships behind the Grow Zambia agenda and was shifting from delivering services directly towards sharing expertise and strengthening Zambian institutions.

**"Growth must be sustainable, resilient and inclusive,"** Terzeon said, linking that to reducing poverty and to resilience against shocks such as El Niño and Ebola. Zambia Monitor reported her saying prosperity rests on macroeconomic stability, effective institutions, accountable government, political pluralism, freedom of speech and the rule of law, and that Zambia has an important role in the mineral supply chains of the global energy transition.

body.text: The ask from the Zambian side

body: Mines and Minerals Development Minister Brenda Tambatamba spoke for the hosts' interest. News Diggers reported her asking for more British investment in mining, energy and critical minerals to help Zambia reach its goal of three million tonnes of copper a year by 2031. Getting there, she said, would need new mineral discoveries, greenfield projects, reliable electricity, stronger local suppliers and efficient regional trade routes. **"Achieving this will require more than expansion of existing mines. It will require new discoveries,"** she said, in the words News Diggers quoted.

Neither outlet reported any new agreement signed at the reception, nor figures for the investment Tambatamba hopes to attract; the speeches set out positions rather than commitments. Zambia Monitor's account notes that the UK's description of itself as a natural partner matched language the President has used, and both outlets place the exchange within the government's Grow Zambia agenda and its 2031 copper target.

stories.title: Chilufya scores, Girumugisha answers, Algeria pull three clear: a 1–1 draw before 44,000 in Ndola leaves Zambia second in Group I, with the return in Bujumbura on Tuesday
stories.excerpt: Edward Chilufya's 64th-minute finish from Albert Kangwanda's pass put Zambia ahead against Burundi at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on Friday 13 November, but Jean Claude Girumugisha equalised nine minutes from time and the Chipolopolo found no winner in five added minutes. Algeria's 1–0 win over Togo in Tizi Ouzou on Saturday puts them on seven points to Zambia's four, with Togo on three and Burundi on two. George Lwandamina said his players failed to reproduce their training form; the squad landed in Bujumbura on Saturday for Tuesday's return.

image.label: Ndola, 1–1
image.caption: A full Levy Mwanawasa Stadium saw Zambia lead for 17 minutes before Burundi levelled.

body: Zambia's Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Burundi at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Friday 13 November ended 1–1, a result that leaves the Chipolopolo second in Group I and three points behind Algeria after the weekend's other match. The gates had been opened to all fans after President Hichilema bought the tickets, and the Football Association of Zambia put the attendance at about 44,000, ZamFoot reported.

The first half was goalless and, in the accounts of ZamFoot and News Diggers, uncomfortable. Goalkeeper Willard Mwanza made two early saves, including from Jean Girumugisha, and News Diggers reported that Burundi wasted a one-on-one in the 38th minute. Albert Kangwanda's free kicks were saved or cleared. George Lwandamina sent on Eliya Mandanji for Derrick Bulaya at the interval, and in the 64th minute Edward Chilufya finished a move built through Kangwanda to put Zambia ahead. A triple substitution in the 77th minute brought on Gift Mphande, Wilson Chisala and Zephania Phiri for Kangwanda, Chilufya and Prince Mumba, but Girumugisha equalised with nine minutes of normal time left, and five added minutes produced no winner.

body.text: The team had been doing very well, training very well, but on the day of the game, they failed to replicate.
body.attribution: George Lwandamina, Zambia coach, speaking after the match in Ndola on Friday 13 November, as reported by ZamFoot

body: Lwandamina told reporters his side had made basic errors, even in ball control, which made the result more painful, and that the equaliser came from a single mistake after the midfield had begun to settle. He said fatigue and injury worries drove his substitutions, with players signalling they could not continue, and that forcing them on would have made the next match harder. FAZ president Keith Mweemba thanked the President for opening the gates and said the association hoped to make such support the norm, adding that he was confident the players would repay the fans in the away fixture.

Algeria beat Togo 1–0 at the Stade Hocine-Aït-Ahmed in Tizi Ouzou on Saturday 14 November, Ramy Bensebaini heading in Anis Hadj Moussa's cross in the 76th minute, Pan Africa Football reported. That leaves Algeria on seven points, Zambia on four, Togo on three and Burundi on two after three rounds. Zambia's results so far are a 2–0 home win over Togo, a 3–1 defeat in Algeria and Friday's draw.

The squad landed at Melchior Ndadaye International Airport in Bujumbura at 12:45 local time on Saturday and is based at the Hotel Club du Lac Tanganyika, ZamFoot reported from a FAZ Media release. The return against Burundi is on Tuesday 17 November; Togo host Algeria in Lomé the same day. The finals are in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania in 2027.

stories.title: Two clear goals or out: the under-23s host Burkina Faso at Heroes at 15:00 today, Patrick Chinyemba's professional debut ends in defeat, and Sporting Lusaka lift the Roberts Cup
stories.excerpt: Chisi Mbewe's Junior Chipolopolo must beat Burkina Faso by two unanswered goals at National Heroes Stadium this afternoon, Sunday 15 November, to overturn a 1–0 first-leg deficit and stay on the road to the 2027 Under-23 AFCON in Egypt, which doubles as the route to the 2028 Olympics. In Philadelphia on Friday, Zambian boxer Patrick Chinyemba lost his first professional bout to the unbeaten Santiago Vazquez, the boxing site No Smoke Boxing reports. And at Nkoloma on Saturday, Sporting Lusaka beat Kafue Celtic 2–0 to win the Roberts Cup with nine men.

image.label: Heroes, 15:00
image.caption: The under-23s need a two-goal win this afternoon to reach the final qualifying round in March.

body: Zambia's under-23 side play the second leg of their Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Burkina Faso at National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka at 15:00 today, Sunday 15 November, needing to win by at least two unanswered goals. Burkina Faso won the first leg 1–0, and ZamFoot reports that the winner over two legs goes through to a final qualifying round in March 2027 against the winner of Mauritania and DR Congo. The tournament, Egypt 2027, also decides Africa's places at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles, which go to the two finalists.

Coach Chisi Mbewe called it a do-or-die game and told his players the first-leg score no longer matters: they must score twice without reply and should not feel the pressure. He urged supporters to fill the stadium as they had filled Levy Mwanawasa for the senior side in Ndola on Friday. Captain Humphrey Bwembya said the squad had put the Ouagadougou defeat behind it. Tickets, sold through Computicket at Shoprite outlets, are K50 for the north and south wings, K100 for the east, K150 for the west and K300 for VIP, ZamFoot reported.

body.text: A hard first night as a professional

body: Patrick Chinyemba's professional debut did not go his way. The boxing website No Smoke Boxing reports from the 2300 Arena in Philadelphia that the Zambian, billed as Patrick Baddo Chinyemba, lost a six-round bantamweight contest to Santiago Vazquez, who came in unbeaten at 5–0 with three knockouts, on Red Owl Boxing's BoxFest XXII card on Friday 13 November. The site reports that Vazquez dropped Chinyemba in the first and third rounds and kept landing left hooks to the final bell, and lists the Zambian's record as 0–1. It does not give the scorecards or the official method of victory, and no report of the result by a Zambian outlet was found; this account rests on that one report.

At Nkoloma Stadium on Saturday 14 November, Sporting Lusaka beat Kafue Celtic 2–0 in the final of the Roberts Cup, a pre-season tournament, ZamFoot reported. Milner Sondashi scored in the first half after a pass from Darius Musonda, and Peter Subakanya sealed it with a solo goal, even though Sporting finished with nine players after left-back Lucky Daka and midfielder Martin Tumbwe were sent off. Kafue Celtic had beaten Game On 4–0 and Sporting had beaten Red Arrows Youth 3–1 in the semi-finals; Game On took third place 3–1 against Red Arrows Youth.

stories.title: No visa, no Puerto Rico: Zambia withdraws from the 75th Miss Universe after its nurse-contestant is caught by US travel restrictions, with Congo out too and Zimbabwe still waiting
stories.excerpt: Miss Universe Zambia has confirmed that its titleholder, a 25-year-old registered nurse crowned on 8 October and named by Zambia Monitor as Pamela Mubanga, will not compete in San Juan on 24 November because she could not obtain a United States visa under the Trump administration's travel restrictions. The organisers said her case 'is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction', not to any personal problem. The Republic of Congo has also withdrawn, and Zimbabwe's Roseanna Hall was still waiting in South Africa.

image.label: No ticket to San Juan
image.caption: Zambia's entrant for the 75th Miss Universe cannot travel because of US visa restrictions on several African countries.

body: Zambia will have no contestant at the 75th Miss Universe pageant. The national franchise confirmed, in a statement reported by Zambia Monitor on Friday 13 November, that its titleholder had withdrawn because she could not obtain a United States visa, and that the problem lay with American travel restrictions rather than anything on her side. Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer reported the decision.

The two outlets give the contestant's name differently: Zambia Monitor calls her Pamela Mubanga, the Zambian Observer Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka. Both describe her as a 25-year-old registered nurse, and Zambia Monitor reports that she was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October 2026. In a statement quoted by Zambia Monitor, the organisers said: **"Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction."** The Observer reported that the organisers expressed their disappointment.

The finale is on 24 November at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan, Puerto Rico, a US territory, and contestants began arriving on 8 November for registration, fittings and pre-pageant events, Zambia Monitor reported. The Zambian Observer said the travel restrictions imposed by the Trump administration were expanded in December 2025 and affect travellers from several African countries. Zambia Monitor cited Presidential Proclamation 10998, in force from 1 January 2026, which places 19 countries under partial restrictions limiting visitor, student, exchange and immigrant visas in certain categories, and noted that it could not itself confirm whether Zambia is among the 19; the Zambian organisers' statement, however, attributes the withdrawal to restrictions affecting Zambian nationals.

The Republic of Congo has withdrawn its representative, Georgina Kambongo, the Zambian Observer reported. Zimbabwe's Roseanna Hall had spent several weeks in South Africa trying to secure a visa and was still waiting on the day she was due to leave for Puerto Rico, saying in an Instagram video cited by the BBC, **"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved."** Miss Universe South Sudan, commenting on Hall's video, put her own chances at 50/50. Zambia Monitor said five other African countries were reported to be in similar difficulty but did not name them.

The Observer framed the episode as a question about how immigration policy now shapes international cultural and sporting events. For Zambia it means a crown won on 8 October will not be seen on the Miss Universe stage this year.

analysis.title: Three petitions move the question from who proposed this to what Parliament does
analysis.body: Until Friday the term-limit argument had a proposal without a document: an idea attributed to a nominated MP, a joint statement from ten defeated candidates against it, and a civil society threat of litigation. The Justice Minister's briefing supplies the missing paper. Three petitions on Article 106(3) are now before the National Assembly, and the executive says it will neither sponsor nor block them. That is a defensible constitutional position: petitioning is a right under Article 88(1), and the Assembly is the right body to receive it. It is also politically convenient, because it leaves the President's own view unstated, which is exactly what Mwiimbu declined to supply. The strongest case for the government is that it has proposed nothing and cannot be asked to oppose what citizens are entitled to raise. The strongest case for its critics is that silence from State House is itself a signal when the ruling party's own members have floated the idea. What to watch: whether the Clerk publishes the petitions and names the petitioners; whether the relevant committee schedules hearings; and whether the President, or the UPND through Haimbe's office, answers the direct question his minister would not.

analysis.title: Gross pay widens NHIMA's base; the State taking the debt is the bigger admission
analysis.body: Moving the 2% deduction from basic to gross pay is the visible part of Cabinet's NHIMA decision, and it is the part workers will notice in January. Where allowances form a large share of a pay packet, the same percentage will yield materially more. But the minister's own framing matters more: he said the scheme was set up on flawed financial grounds and could not meet its obligations. Taking K1.7 billion of supplier debt onto the Treasury, paying dialysis directly, and buying cover for elderly non-contributors and cash-transfer beneficiaries amounts to the State acknowledging that an insurance fund cannot carry universal obligations on a contributory base alone. The case for the package is that providers who have gone unpaid get settled and the fund restarts clean. The case against, from the wage-earner's side, is that it arrives in the same budget as a VAT rise to 16.5%, and that no change to the employer's share has been reported. Unknown so far: the legal instrument that will give effect to the change, how allowances in kind will be treated, and whether NHIMA's benefit package expands to match the larger contribution.

analysis.title: Four points from three is not a crisis, but Bujumbura now carries the weight of the group
analysis.body: A home draw with the side at the bottom of the group is a poor result, and Lwandamina said as much. The arithmetic is less bleak than the mood. Algeria's win in Tizi Ouzou puts them on seven points after three rounds and leaves Zambia on four, Togo on three and Burundi on two, so Zambia remain second and the sides below them are within a point or two. The concern is form rather than position: the coach himself said his players failed to reproduce their training, made basic errors in ball control and conceded from a single mistake once the midfield had settled, and both ZamFoot and News Diggers describe a first half in which Burundi had the better chances. The case for patience is that the substitutions were forced by fatigue and injury, not design, and that the squad is already in Bujumbura with three days to prepare. What to watch on Tuesday: whether Chilufya starts after being withdrawn, whether Mwanza's early saves were the exception or the pattern, and whether a point in Bujumbura is treated as acceptable or as another drop, with Togo hosting Algeria the same day.
